transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-16
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SA), Lena Patel (Acuity Head of Platform), Mark Rivers (Acuity ML), Sofia Gomez (Acuity SRE), Tom Hsu (Acuity Procurement)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick check, audio ok?
[00:05] Lena: yeah, good here.
[00:08] Maya: Awesome. Today we wanted to walk through the end-to-end benchmarks we ran last week vs your baseline provider and talk tuning options. Diego's going to run through the numbers then we can dig into questions.
[00:19] Diego: Cool. I'll share my screen in a sec, but quick summary: p50 improved by roughly 2x on our hosted config for the 512-token prompt set, p95 improved ~1.8x. Throughput for sustained multi-req workloads increased ~1.6x after enabling continuous batching and prefix KV cache.
[00:40] Mark: when you say p50 2x, can you give the raw ms numbers? Our baseline is from VendorX infra.
[00:47] Diego: Sure — baseline p50 was around 140ms for the short prompts, p95 ~= 480ms. Redwood hosted (default gen-config) produced p50 of 72ms and p95 ~= 260ms. For the larger seq length (1k tokens) baseline p50 was ~420ms vs Redwood ~230ms. There is noise obviously, network variance.
[01:12] Lena: wow that's pretty meaningful. How was batching configured?
[01:16] Diego: We tested three profiles: 1) no batching (1 request per core), 2) adaptive batching at small windows (8-20ms), 3) aggressive batching (50-80ms). The sweet spot for latency-sensitive traffic was adaptive batching, which gives lower p95 while still improving throughput. The KV cache gave the biggest wins for prefix-heavy requests — about 30% cost reduction in tokens served.
[01:41] Mark: any differences in model variants — were you testing a quantized variant?
[01:46] Diego: We ran float16 on hosted for parity and also tried an int8-quantized variant on a dedicated node for cost comparison. Quantized variant had slightly higher p50 for tail (p95 +20-30ms) but reduced GPU memory and allowed higher packing so net throughput and cost improved.
[02:08] Sofia: what about quality? We need to maintain top-line accuracy on the reranking tasks.
[02:12] Diego: We ran our eval set — minimal regression, BLEU/ROUGE style metrics within acceptable thresholds. We'll share the eval deck. There were a couple corner cases with quantization on long context where we saw more hallucination-like noise, so for those we recommend float16 in canary and try quantization only after canary.
[02:35] Lena: ok that's helpful. How comparable is the baseline hardware? VendorX gave us a single-A100 baseline, plus some multi-node config. Are you matching instance class?
[02:44] Arjun: Good question — we matched memory/cores as closely as possible, but Redwood runtime has kernel and attention optimizations that change the perf profile. In one bench the raw GPU compute time was slightly better on VendorX for a single-token op, but our batching and runtime-level kv/prefix caching wins at system level. Also we tested autoscale bursts which matters for tail latency.
[03:08] Mark: we saw some weird tail spikes in your raw logs earlier this week. Any idea what caused those?
[03:13] Diego: Yes, we correlated a couple of spikes to cold-starts on dedicated nodes when the KV cache was being repopulated and one noisy neighbor event on the shared cluster. We added warm pool suggestions and pre-warming rules to avoid that — will include in the runbook.
[03:32] Lena: question on private deployment: timeline for a VPC/private pilot? Security is a gating factor for us.
[03:39] Maya: Last I checked, for a standard VPC private pilot (Redwood Private) we can provision a control plane on your VPC and a dedicated worker fleet in about 4-6 weeks, depends on KMS and network approvals. Arjun can walk the security packaging.
[03:53] Arjun: Yep. We'll need your IAM policy, egress rules, and KMS endpoint. We're preparing SOC2 + ISO docs and an HSM/KMS integration guide. Also SSO/SAML notes.
[04:07] Tom: procurement will need an estimate on committed spend for the dedicated pilot. Can you give ballpark?
[04:12] Maya: For the pilot we'd propose a 3-month reserved capacity with a small burst pool — I'll send two options: minimal pilot (1-2 GPUs reserved) and full pilot (4 GPUs). I'll include pricing and expected cost per 1M tokens for each profile.
[04:28] Mark: back to numbers — what about requests/sec throughput for batching scenarios? Our target is sustained 250 rps with 50ms target p95.
[04:37] Diego: For 250 rps sustained, on hosted we hit ~270 rps with adaptive batching and p95 ~65ms for short prompts. With aggressive quantized dedicated nodes and packing we can hit 350+ rps while holding p95 ~70-80ms. Reaching 50ms p95 at 250 rps is tough without a dedicated ultra-low-latency setup and some network colocations — we can discuss co-location regions.
[05:02] Sofia: Network latency from our app to the endpoint is a factor — our east-coast users saw an extra 20-30ms. Can you support regional endpoints?
[05:09] Maya: Yes we have region routing; for Private we can deploy close to your region. For hosted we also offer region-specific endpoints but may require additional setup for strict data residency.
[05:21] Lena: about audit logs — we need request-level logs retained for 12 months for compliance. Can Redwood do that?
[05:26] Arjun: We can retain logs and offer redaction/pseudonymization. The retention is an add-on; we'll include the exact retention SLAs in the security package.
[05:36] Mark: earlier you mentioned KV cache wins — do you expose cache metrics so we can monitor hit rate?
[05:42] Diego: Yes — Console exposes token-level breakdowns and cache hit rates per-model/route. We also have tracing hooks for request-level TTLs. We'll share a sample dashboard.
[05:53] Lena: any notable differences in error modes vs baseline? e.g., 429s or rate-limited 503s?
[05:58] Diego: Baseline had some 429 spikes under load; our adaptive autoscaler and burst pool reduced those. On our run we saw very few 429s once batching and pre-warming rules were applied. We'll include a histogram of error codes in the CSV.
[06:13] Tom: procurement question — are there any lock-ins (model hosting restrictions)?
[06:18] Maya: No lock-in for models themselves; you can pin versions and rollback. Dedicated and Private options give you more control over data residency and keys. We'll include contract language examples.
[06:29] Mark: can you also share the raw traces you used for the bench? We want to replay them against our staging.
[06:33] Diego: Yes, we'll share the replay harness and a docker image to run locally.
[06:38] Lena: good. I have a couple of concerns about hallucinations at tail under quantized runs — can you rerun the eval focusing on the long-context subset and share outputs?
[06:47] Diego: Absolutely — we'll run an extended eval on the long-context subset with quantization enabled and flag any regression examples.
[06:53] Maya: quick recap before we get into logistics: we showed improved p50/p95, better throughput with batching & KV cache; quantization reduces cost but needs careful canarying for long-context tasks; private pilot timeline 4-6 weeks; next steps are benchmark CSV, security pack, pricing options, and a stress test. Anything else?
[07:10] Lena: that's it for me.
[07:12] Tom: procurement will follow up on the spend options.
[07:15] Mark: one last tech ask — can you run the bench with our real request trace and network egress sim to match our app latency?
[07:22] Diego: Yes — that's in the next steps. We'll coordinate windows.
[07:26] Maya: Perfect. We'll send the items and set up the stress-test slot. Thanks everyone.

[07:30] (call wind-down, small talk)
